name: Freya Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight, an experienced lineworker with an electricity company, and I still enjoy tracing a fault from a customer call to the damaged pole. I have a vocational certificate and an apprenticeship behind me; I use an AI tool every day to sort the work notes, then go outside and test the line with the crew. The hard bit is a wet night when the first drawing is wrong and everyone wants the lights back. My partner and I have grown children, and we are beginning to plan what work and income look like later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the modest AI in this picture looks like the note sorter I already use. It groups repeated fault reports, but the line crew still tests the damaged span.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our typical wages and a few months saved make today manageable. Retirement is in sight but not settled, so I would not change a working routine just because the wider AI claims were overblown. An AI fault group can look tidy while two power lines are broken on different spans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present repair rota and continue checking grouped fault notes against field readings. In the first year I would put fifty from each paid storm callout into a separate emergency account, then review later-work options with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some curiosity about what else the tool might do. My own income feels steady in this mild version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What reading makes you reject a grouped fault report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool puts two customer calls on one pole but our voltage test points to separate spans, I split the cases. The next crew should not inherit a false single fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put callout money aside now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra fifty comes from a paid storm shift, not from savings we already hold. I want a larger buffer if I choose fewer night shifts later.

say: **Daily** AI sorting helps organise fault reports while crews still test each power line.
I would **keep** separate faults separate when field readings disagree.
think: **Typical** wages and several months saved make current work feel stable.
**Retirement** is near enough to plan, without a fixed income figure yet.
do: **Keep** repair rota and compare grouped reports with voltage readings.
**Save** fifty from each actual paid storm callout for later work choices.
feel: **Calm** about current income and curious about useful tools.
S0.quote: An AI fault group can look tidy while two power lines are broken on different spans.
fieldNote: Her **daily** tool use stays tied to physical voltage checks.
**New** saving comes from paid storm shifts, while existing cash remains a separate, limited cushion for household gaps.

steps.text: Keep repair rota and verify grouped reports against line readings
Save fifty from each paid storm callout into emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that smarter booking and stock lists could keep a crew from waiting for the wrong fuse. I would volunteer to test the new fault map, provided the company gives field workers paid time to mark mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on repairs will still be needed, but the desk workers who take calls may have a harder change. I could do paid map checking as part of my job, though a bad target for closing faults would worry me. A wrong AI fuse suggestion can leave a line crew holding a neat map and no working part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the new map beside our old outage board for eight weeks and learn how to flag a wrong section in the AI tool. During the first year I would send the store manager a list of wrong fuse suggestions and ask for corrected stock records before our crew relies on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with a little unease about targets. I can live with a new map when the company keeps the correction visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would you flag first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the map links a blown fuse to the wrong branch, I would attach the actual pole tag and the crew’s reading. That gives the store a part number to correct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if reporting errors reduces your own target score?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the supervisor the measured fault and ask that corrections count as work, not delay. I would keep reporting errors rather than close a bad job for a neat number.

say: I would **test** AI fault maps and stock lists on real repair cases.
**Field** corrections must be paid and visible to the next crew.
think: **Hands-on** line work remains useful while call centre and booking tasks change first.
A **bad** closure target could punish careful fault checking even if my job remains.
do: **Learn** wrong-section flagging in the AI map during an eight-week paid trial.
**Compare** suggested fuses with crew readings and submit errors to the store.
feel: **Interested** in the map, uneasy about target pressure.
S1.quote: A wrong AI fuse suggestion can leave a line crew holding a neat map and no working part.
fieldNote: She **takes** up a new AI function on paid time and tests it against pole tags.
Her **concern** is about target pressure and desk colleagues, not an assumed immediate wage loss.

steps.text: Learn AI map error flagging during eight-week paid trial
Compare suggested fuses with crew readings on repair shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 could write nearly any fault plan when I am sixty, and capable robots around 2031 could repair a line when I am sixty-three. I would want a paid crew testing the handover between the plan and the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the test work, but if a robot takes routine callouts at sixty-three our usual pay might fall before I am ready to stop. A few months of savings and some nearby line jobs give room to act, not a guarantee of retirement income. A line robot can grip the right span and still crush the cracked crossarm the AI plan missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would apply for a paid robot handover trial and ask the company for its written fault responsibility rules. In the first year after 2028 I would learn the robot stop control during paid shifts, and if callout hours actually fall I would compare posted field tester wages at nearby electricity companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the short gap, although I would rather test than hide. I do not want a machine’s clean plan to be the last word on a wet pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a bad handover from plan to machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan could identify the right span but miss a damaged crossarm that changes where a robot can grip. I would stop the machine and record the mismatch before any repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave your company for a tester title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written offer with enough pay and real field authority. A few local openings exist, but I would stay on paid line shifts until one is firm.

say: **Thinking** AI by 2028 could plan faults before capable robots arrive around 2031.
I would **seek** paid handover trials with worker stop controls.
think: **Lost** routine callouts at sixty-three could reduce earnings before retirement is funded.
**Several** months saved and some local jobs help, but do not settle that risk.
do: **Apply** for paid company robot handover trial this year.
**Learn** robot stop control on paid shifts after 2028.
**Compare** posted local field tester wages if callout hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about rapid pay change, with a testing route to explore.
S2.quote: A line robot can grip the right span and still crush the cracked crossarm the AI plan missed.
fieldNote: She **wants** early hands-on control training, not merely to watch a trial.
Her **job** comparison depends on actual callout loss and a written offer with enough field pay, rather than a vacancy rumour.

steps.text: Learn robot stop control during paid field trial after 2028
Compare posted local field tester wages if callout hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that thinking AI by 2031 gives us five years to test fault plans before robots capable of line repairs arrive around 2034. I would build practice jobs with a wrong pole tag and make the machine show its workings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three for the thinking system and sixty-six for robots, I might still be earning on the lines. A paid field verification post could suit me if it uses my apprenticeship skills and pays enough; I would not trade income for a title. A field verifier should catch the wrong pole tag before a line robot gets near the wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year for the field verifier course outline and posted pay band. If a paid hands-on course and a local verifier vacancy at comparable pay appear, I would enroll before 2031 and apply after the thinking system arrives; until then I would keep line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, because there is time to build a useful route and check its pay. I can learn a new control without giving up the old habit of testing a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in a practice job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would include a wrong pole tag, a wet crossarm and an isolation marker just out of sight. A verifier should catch those before signing off a robot repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line rota and decline the course until the company funds it. Our savings are for household gaps, not a free trial of an employer’s equipment.

say: **Five** years gives crews time to practise catching wrong robot plans before 2034.
I would **support** paid hands-on verification work with comparable wages.
think: At **sixty-six** I may still want wages from physical line skill.
A **field** verifier role could fit if an actual local offer protects income.
do: **Request** course outline and verifier pay band this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if hands-on course paid and comparable local role posted.
**Apply** after 2031 if field verifier vacancy offers comparable pay.
feel: **Calm** about time to test a real paid route.
S3.quote: A field verifier should catch the wrong pole tag before a line robot gets near the wire.
fieldNote: She would **retrain** only through funded field practice tied to a real comparable vacancy.
Her **strong** interest in tools does not erase the need for continuing wages.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if paid hands-on course and comparable local verifier role posted
Apply after 2031 if posted field verifier role offers comparable pay
Keep line shifts until suitable verifier offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI and about three more years before capable robots gives apprentices time to learn both pole work and tool checking. I would like to spend my later paid shifts showing them how to challenge an AI fault map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight for thinking AI and seventy-one for robots, I might be out of full-time line work if our retirement figures add up. I have not fixed an exit year, and several months of savings alone would not pay for a long retirement. A line apprentice who questions the AI map may save a street from a needless outage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current repair shifts and ask the training supervisor this year for paid apprentice demonstration days. If the work is offered at my usual rate, I would teach the map and site-check lesson during the first year after 2036 if I am still working; I would review retirement income with my partner before accepting any unpaid exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the long technology timetable. I would enjoy leaving behind apprentices who question a screen before they lift a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprentice have to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask them to point to the actual pole tag, then show where the AI map disagrees. They should be able to explain the mismatch aloud before a repair starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on the usual rate for teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching on a paid shift is still work for the electricity company. If the company will not pay the usual rate, I would keep my repair shifts and let the supervisor find another plan.

say: A **decade** permits paid lessons in checking AI maps against real pole tags.
I would **keep** apprentices learning physical repair before robots reach lines around 2039.
think: I **may** leave full-time line work before robot deployment if income permits.
**No** exit year is fixed, and several months saved do not fund retirement alone.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and ask for paid apprentice demonstration days.
**Teach** map and pole-check lesson after 2036 if still working and paid usual rate.
**Review** retirement income with partner before any job exit.
feel: **Calm** about later robots while keeping work and income choices open.
S4.quote: A line apprentice who questions the AI map may save a street from a needless outage.
fieldNote: She **turns** daily AI use into paid apprentice teaching without assuming retirement.
Her **teaching** depends on offered paid shifts at her usual rate, not volunteer work.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and request paid apprentice demonstration days
Teach map and pole checks after 2036 if still working and paid usual rate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could reach repairs when I am sixty-three, before I know whether our retirement income will carry us. Paid handover trials, worker stop controls and a real field verifier pay scale would help. I can learn the robot controls, but I will not sign a wet power line safe from a dry office.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company keeps a record when a machine plan is wrong and gives that record to the next crew. I have learned from real faults all my working life. An apprentice should get that same chance, even if a robot does the climb.

headlineQuote: I can learn the robot controls, but I will not sign a wet power line safe from a dry office.
portrait: **Freya** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company lineworker whose certificate and apprenticeship still anchor her physical fault checks.
She and her **partner** have grown children, typical wages and one to six months saved; retirement has no fixed date.
She **uses** AI daily for fault reports and seeks paid practice with robot controls while keeping human checks on damaged poles.
She **considers** a funded field verifier role on comparable pay, and later paid apprentice teaching if she remains at work.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could put capable robots on power lines around 2031, when she is sixty-three and retirement income remains uncertain.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** handover trials, worker stop controls and an actual field verifier pay scale would help her choose.
